findings.title: `organization_context.member` can be None, causing AttributeError on every request
findings.body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated unconditionally for every GET, before the `use_optimized` check. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is `None` whenever the caller is not an organization member — e.g. requests authenticated with an org-level/integration token (where `request.user` is an AnonymousUser and `is_superuser` is False), or a staff/superuser-less service account. In those cases the short-circuit does not fire and `None.has_global_access` raises `AttributeError`, turning a previously working audit-log listing into an unhandled 500. Guard with `organization_context.member and organization_context.member.has_global_access`, and only compute the flag when `use_optimized` is true.

findings.title: Authorization gate does not restrict the feature to administrators
findings.body: The comment says the new pagination path is for "authorized administrators", but the check is `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`. Two problems: (1) `request.user.is_superuser` is the raw DB flag; Sentry requires `is_active_superuser(request)` (or the staff equivalent) so that superuser powers only apply within an elevated/validated superuser session — using the raw flag bypasses that elevation requirement; (2) `member.has_global_access` is not an admin signal at all: it is true for ordinary members in organizations with open membership / global access, so essentially any regular org member can turn on the "admin-only" code path by appending `?optimized_pagination=true`. The gate should use an explicit permission/scope check.

findings.title: Negative queryset slicing raises ValueError; the "Django handles it" comment is wrong
findings.body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset` (and often a negative `stop`, since `stop = start_offset + limit + extra`). Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly rejects negative start/stop values with `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`; there is no SQL equivalent of a negative OFFSET. So the inline comment "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is factually false, and any request carrying a cursor with a negative offset on this path returns an unhandled 500. Since cursor strings are fully client-controlled (`Cursor.from_string` accepts negative offsets), this is a trivially reachable error/DoS vector. The whole negative-offset branch should be removed, or negative offsets rejected with `BadPaginationError`.

findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot handle datetime sort keys, which is what the audit-log endpoint uses
findings.body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `int(math.floor(getattr(item, self.key)))` and `value_from_cursor` returns `cursor.value` unchanged — i.e. it copies `Paginator`'s numeric-key semantics. The only caller, `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint`, instantiates it with `order_by="-datetime"` on `AuditLogEntry`, whose `datetime` field is a `datetime` object: `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime`. Even if the first page somehow succeeded, `value_from_cursor` would hand an integer to `build_queryset`, which injects it into `WHERE "datetime" <= %s` against a timestamp column, producing a database error. The optimized path therefore fails for every request that reaches it; it needs `DateTimePaginator`-style key/value conversion (or should subclass `DateTimePaginator`).

findings.title: Cursors are not interchangeable between the two paginators selected by a query param
findings.body: The endpoint switches between `DateTimePaginator` (cursor value = epoch milliseconds) and `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (cursor value = floor/ceil of the raw sort value) based on the client-supplied `optimized_pagination` flag. A cursor minted by one paginator is meaningless to the other, so a client that follows a `Link` header while the flag changes (or that caches cursors) will get wrong pages, skipped/duplicated rows, or a query error. Pagination state must not depend on a mutable request flag; pick one cursor encoding or namespace the cursors.

findings.title: BasePaginator silently clamps negative forward offsets, changing behavior for every paginated endpoint
findings.body: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes the shared `BasePaginator.get_result` used by most paginated Sentry endpoints: a forward cursor with a negative offset, which previously surfaced as an error from Django slicing, now silently returns the first page's rows. That masks malformed/tampered cursors and can produce duplicated results across pages. Note also that the clamp is deliberately not applied when `cursor.is_prev`, so the previous-page path still crashes with `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` — the stated justification ("the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions") is incorrect. Invalid offsets should raise `BadPaginationError` consistently for both directions.

findings.title: No tests for the new paginator or the new endpoint branch
findings.body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (including its negative-offset branch) and the new `optimized_pagination` branch in `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` ship with no tests, and the behavior change in `BasePaginator.get_result` (offset clamping) is likewise untested. Basic tests would have caught the `math.floor(datetime)` TypeError, the negative-slice `ValueError`, and the `organization_context.member is None` AttributeError. Add paginator unit tests for negative/zero/positive offsets plus endpoint tests covering member, non-member-token and superuser callers.

findings.title: Comment documents a non-existent feature of Cursor
findings.body: The added comment claims "Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios", but no code changed here — `int(offset)` has always accepted any integer and nothing validates or makes use of negative offsets. The comment asserts that negative offsets are a supported, intentional capability, which is false: every consumer eventually feeds the offset into a Django queryset slice, which rejects negative values. This will mislead future readers into producing negative-offset cursors. Remove the comment or, better, add explicit validation that rejects negative offsets.
